questions.sec: Ascites: definition and onset proportions · p1005
questions.q: Ascites is defined as:
opts: Fluid trapped in the bowel lumen
Edema fluid of the hepatic capsule
Free fluid in the peritoneal cavity
questions.exp: Definition: free fluid in peritoneal cavity. (Book p1005)

questions.sec: Ascites: definition and onset proportions · p1005
questions.q: Ascites is also defined as:
opts: A sign of chronic liver failure only
questions.exp: Definition bullets: free fluid in peritoneal cavity; 1st sign of decompensation. (Book p1005)

questions.sec: Ascites: definition and onset proportions · p1005
questions.q: Match the onset proportions — 1) Ascites due to portal hypertension 2) Ascites due to peritoneal causes 3) PHTN from cirrhosis 4) PHTN without cirrhosis … A) 85% B) 90% C) 10% D) 5%
questions.exp: Onset: 90% d/t portal hypertension (PHTN), 10% d/t peritoneal causes; of PHTN, 85% cirrhosis and 5% no cirrhosis. (Book p1005)

questions.sec: Ascites: definition and onset proportions · p1005
questions.q: In a hospital series of 200 new ascites patients, applying only epidemiologic proportions, how many would have portal-hypertensive ascites due to cirrhosis?
questions.exp: 200 × 90% = 180 portal-hypertensive; 85% of those (153) are cirrhotic per the p1005 onset tree. (Book p1005)

questions.sec: Fulminant hepatitis and the SAAG quadrant map · p1005
questions.q: The feature of ascites in fulminant hepatitis is:
opts: Ascites with a chronic PHTN picture
questions.exp: Fulminant hepatitis: ascites without chronic picture (PHTN). (Book p1005)

questions.sec: Fulminant hepatitis and the SAAG quadrant map · p1005
questions.q: All but one of the following are listed as causes of fulminant hepatitis . The odd one out is:
questions.exp: Listed causes: paracetamol / alcohol / mushroom / rat killer poisoning; aflatoxin is not on the p1005 list. (Book p1005)

questions.sec: Fulminant hepatitis and the SAAG quadrant map · p1005
questions.q: SAAG (serum ascites albumin gradient) = S. albumin minus:
questions.exp: SAAG: serum ascites albumin gradient = S. albumin − ascitic fluid albumin (AFA). (Book p1005)

questions.sec: Fulminant hepatitis and the SAAG quadrant map · p1005
questions.q: A SAAG ≥ 1.1 defines high-SAAG ascites, which account for what proportion of ascites ()?
questions.exp: ≥ 1.1 : high SAAG ascites (90%) d/t PHTN. (Book p1005)

questions.sec: Fulminant hepatitis and the SAAG quadrant map · p1005
questions.q: A SAAG < 1.1 defines low-SAAG ascites (10%), due to:
questions.exp: < 1.1 : low SAAG ascites (10%) d/t peritoneal membrane permeability. (Book p1005)

questions.sec: Fulminant hepatitis and the SAAG quadrant map · p1005
questions.q: Match the four SAAG × protein quadrants — 1) High SAAG, high protein 2) High SAAG, low protein 3) Low SAAG, high protein 4) Low SAAG, low protein … A) ↓ protein synthesis, ↑ loss : nephrotic syndrome B) Through hepatic vein — BCS (Budd–Chiari) C) Any peritoneal cause, m/c : peritoneal CA D) ↑ Sinusoidal pressure
questions.exp: High SAAG + high protein (↓AFA, ↑protein): through hepatic vein — BCS; high SAAG + low protein (↓AFA, ↓protein): ↑ sinusoidal pressure; low SAAG + high protein (↑AFA, ↑protein): any peritoneal cause, m/c peritoneal CA; low SAAG + low protein (↓protein synthesis, ↑loss): nephrotic syndrome. (Book p1005)

questions.sec: Fulminant hepatitis and the SAAG quadrant map · p1005
questions.q: In the high-SAAG, high-protein quadrant, what directional changes in serum-ascites albumin difference and fluid protein concentration occur?
questions.exp: High SAAG, high protein: ↓ AFA, ↑ protein (through hepatic vein — BCS). (Book p1005)

questions.sec: Fulminant hepatitis and the SAAG quadrant map · p1005
questions.q: ‘In low-SAAG, high-protein ascites the ascitic fluid albumin (AFA) is reduced.’
opts: False — that quadrant is ↑ AFA with ↑ protein (peritoneal causes, m/c peritoneal CA)
True — AFA is reduced in every low-SAAG pattern
False — the AFA is normal in peritoneal disease
True, but only in nephrotic syndrome
questions.exp: Low SAAG, high protein: ↑ AFA, ↑ protein (cause: any peritoneal cause, m/c peritoneal CA). (Book p1005)

questions.sec: Fulminant hepatitis and the SAAG quadrant map · p1005
questions.q: A paracentesis gives SAAG 2.0 g/dL and ascitic protein 4.0 g/dL, with the AFA well below the serum albumin. Which quadrant and aetiology fit?
opts: High SAAG, high protein — Budd–Chiari through the hepatic vein
High SAAG, low protein — sinusoidal pressure
Low SAAG, high protein — peritoneal CA
Low SAAG, low protein — nephrotic syndrome
questions.exp: SAAG ≥ 1.1 + high ascitic protein (↓AFA, ↑protein) = the BCS quadrant, not the usual cirrhotic low-protein pattern. (Book p1005)

questions.sec: The mechanism of ascites: the NO → retention chain · p1006
questions.q: The mechanism chain begins with nitric oxide (NO) causing:
questions.exp: Mechanism: nitric oxide (NO) → splanchnic vasodilation. (Book p1006)

questions.sec: The mechanism of ascites: the NO → retention chain · p1006
questions.q: Match the systems stimulated by ↓ effective intravascular volume — 1) Hormonal 2) Neural 3) Renin–angiotensin … A) RAAS B) Sympathetic nervous system (SNS) C) ADH
questions.exp: ↓ effective intravascular volume stimulates ADH, the sympathetic nervous system (SNS) and RAAS. (Book p1006)

questions.sec: The mechanism of ascites: the NO → retention chain · p1006
questions.q: ‘The fall in effective intravascular volume in the cirrhotic cascade is caused by splanchnic vasoconstriction.’
opts: False — it follows splanchnic vasodilation by NO
False — the volume falls before any vascular change
True, but only after RAAS activation
questions.exp: Chain: NO → splanchnic vasodilation → ↓ effective intravascular volume → ADH/SNS/RAAS stimulation → ↑ salt + H₂O retention → ascites. (Book p1006)

questions.sec: The mechanism of ascites: the NO → retention chain · p1006
questions.q: All but one of the following are the three printed downstream states of ascites . The odd one out is:
questions.exp: The ascites arrow branches to refractory ascites, hyponatremia and hepatorenal syndrome (HRS); encephalopathy is not in this p1006 branch. (Book p1006)

questions.sec: The mechanism of ascites: the NO → retention chain · p1006
questions.q: A cirrhotic with tense ascites has serum Na⁺ 124 mmol/L and a creatinine that has risen from 1.1 to 1.9 mg/dL over a week. Two of the three downstream states are present. Which pair?
questions.exp: Na⁺ 124 = hyponatremia; the rising creatinine with ascites = the hepatorenal syndrome arm of the p1006 branch. (Book p1006)

questions.sec: The mechanism of ascites: the NO → retention chain · p1006
questions.q: In the pathophysiologic cascade of chronic liver disease, persistent renal retention of sodium and water directly manifests as:
questions.exp: Increased salt and water retention directly produces peritoneal ascites. (Book p1006)

questions.sec: Chylous vs pseudochylous ascites: the table · p1006
questions.q: Match the chylous column of the comparative table — 1) Onset 2) Cause 3) Triglycerides 4) Lipoprotein electrophoresis … A) Chylomicrons present B) Sudden C) > 110 mg/dL D) Trauma
questions.exp: Chylous: sudden onset, trauma, milky-white (or yellow to bloody), lymphocytosis, triglycerides > 110 mg/dL, chylomicrons present. (Book p1006)

questions.sec: Chylous vs pseudochylous ascites: the table · p1006
questions.q: Match the pseudochylous column of the comparative table — 1) Onset 2) Cause 3) Microscopic examination 4) Appearance … A) Milky or greenish, metallic sheen B) Mixed cellular reaction, cholesterol crystals C) Gradual D) Rheumatoid arthritis / TB
questions.exp: Pseudochylous: gradual onset, RA/TB, milky or greenish with metallic sheen, mixed cellular reaction with cholesterol crystals, triglycerides < 50 mg/dL, chylomicrons absent with cholesterol crystals (+) on electrophoresis. (Book p1006)

questions.sec: Chylous vs pseudochylous ascites: the table · p1006
questions.q: In the comparative table, the triglyceride level that defines chylous ascites is:
questions.exp: Triglycerides: chylous > 110 mg/dL versus pseudochylous < 50 mg/dL. (Book p1006)

questions.sec: Chylous vs pseudochylous ascites: the table · p1006
questions.q: ‘Pseudochylous ascites shows chylomicrons on lipoprotein electrophoresis.’
opts: False — chylomicrons are absent and cholesterol crystals are (+)
False — pseudochylous shows neither chylomicrons nor crystals
questions.exp: Pseudochylous lipoprotein electrophoresis: chylomicrons absent, cholesterol crystals (+). (Book p1006)

questions.sec: Chylous vs pseudochylous ascites: the table · p1006
questions.q: A patient 48 h after an aorto-iliac procedure develops milky-white ascites; the fluid shows lymphocytosis and triglycerides 150 mg/dL. Per this is:
opts: Low-SAAG ascites due to peritoneal CA
questions.exp: Sudden onset after trauma, milky-white, lymphocytosis and TG > 110 mg/dL = chylous. (Book p1006)

questions.sec: Chylous vs pseudochylous ascites: the table · p1006
questions.q: The pseudochylous ascitic fluid's characteristic appearance is:
opts: Milky or greenish with a metallic sheen
questions.exp: Appearance: chylous — milky-white or yellow to bloody; pseudochylous — milky or greenish, metallic sheen. (Book p1006)

questions.sec: Fluid tapping and the grading–treatment table · p1006
questions.q: The paracentesis site is the left lower quadrant, ___ cm cephalad and ___ cm medial to the ASIS:
questions.exp: Fluid tapping: left lower quadrant 3 cm cephalad, 2 cm medial to ASIS; point of maximal dullness on percussion. (Book p1006)

questions.sec: Fluid tapping and the grading–treatment table · p1006
questions.q: An alternative landmark for the tapping site is:
opts: Mid-clavicular line at the costal margin
The point of maximal dullness on percussion
questions.exp: Second bullet: point of maximal dullness on percussion. (Book p1006)

questions.sec: Fluid tapping and the grading–treatment table · p1006
questions.q: Grade 1 ascites is defined as mild ascites that is:
questions.exp: Grade 1: mild ascites, only detectable by ultrasound; treatment — no treatment. (Book p1006)

questions.sec: Fluid tapping and the grading–treatment table · p1006
questions.q: Grade 2 ascites is defined as moderate ascites evident by:
opts: Moderate symmetrical distension of the abdomen
questions.exp: Grade 2: moderate ascites evident by moderate symmetrical distension of the abdomen. (Book p1006)

questions.sec: Fluid tapping and the grading–treatment table · p1006
questions.q: Match the grade-2 diuretic ladder — 1) First diuretic 2) Its starting dose 3) Added on no response 4) Its starting dose … A) Lasix 40 mg/d B) Spironolactone 100 mg/d C) 40 mg/d D) 100 mg/d
questions.exp: Diuretics: spironolactone 100 mg/d (max 400 mg/d); on no response Lasix 40 mg/d (max 160 mg/d); then refractory ascites. (Book p1006)

questions.sec: Fluid tapping and the grading–treatment table · p1006
questions.q: The maximum daily doses printed are spironolactone 400 mg/d and Lasix:
questions.exp: Lasix 40 mg/d (max dose : 160 mg/d); spironolactone 100 mg/d (max dose 400 mg/d). (Book p1006)

questions.sec: Fluid tapping and the grading–treatment table · p1006
questions.q: Grade 2 ascites management includes dietary restriction of sodium intake to:
questions.exp: Grade 2 treatment: restriction of sodium intake 2 g/day — degraded in print as 'a g/day'. (Book p1006)

questions.sec: Fluid tapping and the grading–treatment table · p1006
questions.q: Grade 3 ascites (large, marked distension) is initially managed by:
opts: Strict dietary sodium and fluid restriction without any paracentesis
Large-volume paracentesis, then sodium restriction + diuretics (unless refractory)
High-dose spironolactone monotherapy alone titrated up to 400 mg daily
Primary emergent TIPSS placement as the initial therapeutic procedure
questions.exp: Grade 3: large volume paracentesis followed by restriction of sodium intake and diuretics (unless refractory ascites); on no response → TIPSS. (Book p1006)

questions.sec: Fluid tapping and the grading–treatment table · p1006
questions.q: In grade-3 management, TIPSS is reached after:
opts: No response to paracentesis + sodium restriction + diuretics
questions.exp: Grade 3 arrow: no response → TIPSS (Transjugular Intrahepatic Porto Systemic Shunt). (Book p1006)

questions.sec: Fluid tapping and the grading–treatment table · p1006
questions.q: The closing line under ascites grading recommendations instructs:
opts: Always look for JVP for constrictions
questions.exp: Bottom line: always look for JVP for constrictions — i.e., check the JVP for constrictive pericarditis in a patient with ascites. (Book p1006)

questions.q: What are the minimal free peritoneal fluid volumes required sequentially for ultrasonographic detection, clinical shifting dullness, and eliciting a fluid thrill?
questions.exp: Peritoneal fluid detection thresholds are: <100 mL on ultrasonography (USG), 500 mL on clinical examination for shifting dullness, and 1.5 L for elicitation of a fluid thrill. (Book p1007)

questions.q: By definition in decompensated chronic liver disease, refractory ascites refers to peritoneal fluid accumulation that exhibits:
opts: Secondary bacterial infection following diagnostic paracentesis
Development of acute intrinsic tubular necrosis during diuretics
No therapeutic response to maximum doses of diuretic medications
Persistent recurrence despite weekly large-volume paracenteses
questions.exp: Refractory ascites is defined as peritoneal fluid accumulation that shows no response to maximum doses of diuretics (spironolactone up to 400 mg/day plus furosemide up to 160 mg/day). (Book p1007)

questions.q: Following large-volume paracentesis (LVP) for tense ascites, which adjunctive intervention should routinely be administered to preserve effective circulating volume?
questions.exp: Large volume paracentesis (LVP) should be followed by intravenous albumin replacement to prevent post-paracentesis circulatory dysfunction, noted in text as expensive. (Book p1007)

questions.q:
Match each diagnostic modality for ascitic fluid detection with its corresponding minimum fluid threshold:
1. Ultrasonography (USG)
2. Shifting dullness
3. Fluid thrill
questions.exp: Ultrasonography detects free fluid at volumes <100 mL; clinical shifting dullness requires 500 mL; elicitation of a fluid thrill requires 1.5 L of peritoneal fluid. (Book p1007)

questions.q: A 52-year-old man with decompensated alcoholic cirrhosis presents with massive abdominal distension. On examination, a prominent fluid thrill is elicited. Based on physical diagnostic thresholds, what is the minimum volume of free ascitic fluid present?
opts: Around 500 to 750 mL of peritoneal fluid
Strictly less than 100 mL of fluid
At least 1.5 L of free peritoneal fluid
questions.exp: A fluid thrill requires at least 1.5 L of free peritoneal fluid to be elicited clinically. Shifting dullness requires 500 mL, whereas USG can detect volumes <100 mL. (Book p1007)

questions.q: What is the most common causative organism and bacterial class responsible for spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (SBP)?
questions.exp: The primary cause of spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (SBP) is Gram-negative bacteria, most commonly Escherichia coli. (Book p1007)

questions.q: In the diagnostic criteria for spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (SBP), the ascitic fluid analysis must demonstrate a total WBC count of at least ________ or a polymorphonuclear (PMN) neutrophil count of at least ________.
questions.exp: Diagnostic criteria for SBP require: (1) Ascitic fluid WBC ≥500 cells/mL OR PMNs ≥250 cells/mL, (2) positive ascitic fluid culture, and (3) no surgically treatable source of infection. (Book p1007)

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT one of the three established diagnostic criteria for spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (SBP)?
opts: Positive monobacterial culture from ascitic fluid inoculation
Absence of any surgically treatable intra-abdominal infection source
Ascitic fluid serum-ascites albumin gradient (SAAG) less than 1.1 g/dL
Ascitic fluid WBC count ≥500 cells/mL or PMN count ≥250 cells/mL
questions.exp: The 3 criteria for SBP are: (1) ascitic fluid WBC ≥500 cells/mL OR PMNs ≥250 cells/mL, (2) positive culture, and (3) absence of a surgically treatable source of infection. SAAG <1.1 g/dL is not a criterion (cirrhotic ascites has high SAAG ≥1.1). (Book p1007)

questions.q: A 58-year-old cirrhotic patient presents with fever and diffuse abdominal pain. Diagnostic paracentesis reveals an ascitic fluid PMN count of 380 cells/mL (elevated). Ascitic fluid cultures show no bacterial growth at 48 hours, and surgical abdominal sources are ruled out. This entity represents:
opts: Culture-negative neutrocytic ascites (CNNA): criteria 1 and 3 present, 2 absent
Monobacterial non-neutrocytic ascites (MNNA): criteria 2 and 3 present, 1 absent
Secondary bacterial peritonitis requiring emergent exploratory laparotomy
Pseudochylous ascites secondary to thoracic duct obstruction
questions.exp: Culture Negative Neutrocytic Ascites (CNNA) is defined by presence of criteria 1 (PMN ≥250) and 3 (no surgical source), with absence of criterion 2 (culture negative). It represents a milder degree of SBP seen in patients with minimal immunity and good opsonization. (Book p1007)

questions.q:
Match each variant of SBP with its criteria profile and characteristic microbiology:
1. Culture Negative Neutrocytic Ascites (CNNA)
2. Monobacterial Non-Neutrocytic Ascites (MNNA)
opts: 1: Criteria 1+3 present (2 absent); 2: Criteria 1+2 present (3 absent), Polymicrobial > Monomicrobial
1: Criteria 1+3 present (2 absent); 2: Criteria 2+3 present (1 absent), Gram-positive > Gram-negative
1: Criteria 2+3 present (1 absent); 2: Criteria 1+3 present (2 absent), Gram-negative > Gram-positive
1: Criteria 1+2 present (3 absent); 2: Criteria 1+3 present (2 absent), Anaerobic > Aerobic
questions.exp: CNNA has criteria 1+3 present (PMN elevated, no surgical source) and criterion 2 absent (culture negative). MNNA has criteria 2+3 present (culture positive, no surgical source) and criterion 1 absent (PMN <250/mL), with Gram-positive organisms predominating over Gram-negative. (Book p1007)

questions.q: True or False: Differentials of SBP criteria such as CNNA and MNNA represent milder degrees of SBP observed in patients possessing minimal host immunity combined with good opsonization capacity.
opts: False: Severe fulminant peritonitis observed only in patients lacking opsonization
False: Iatrogenic contamination artifacts occurring strictly after repeated taps
False: Secondary surgical catastrophes requiring emergency surgical peritoneal toilet
True: Milder SBP spectrum seen with minimal immunity and good opsonization
questions.exp: As documented under differentials of criteria, CNNA and MNNA represent a milder degree of SBP seen in patients with minimal immunity plus good opsonization (+). (Book p1007)

questions.q: In monobacterial non-neutrocytic ascites (MNNA), how does the microbiological profile characteristically contrast with classic SBP?
opts: Fungal hyphae such as Candida albicans predominate over bacterial pathogens
Gram-positive organisms are isolated more frequently than Gram-negative organisms
Polymicrobial anaerobic enteric flora predominate over single aerobes
Strict anaerobes such as Clostridium species account for nearly all isolates
questions.exp: In MNNA, isolated pathogens characteristically show Gram-positive organisms > Gram-negative organisms, contrasting with classic SBP where Gram-negative E. coli predominates. (Book p1007)

questions.q: In a patient with ascites presenting with acute peritonitis, which triad of ascitic fluid findings strongly points to secondary surgical peritonitis rather than spontaneous bacterial peritonitis?
opts: Protein >3 g/dL, glucose >120 mg/dL, and absence of peritoneal neutrophils
Protein <0.5 g/dL, glucose <10 mg/dL, and elevated amylase without LDH
Protein >1 g/dL, glucose <50 mg/dL, and markedly elevated LDH (LDH ↑↑)
Protein <1 g/dL, glucose >100 mg/dL, and normal peritoneal LDH level
questions.exp: As noted in the book, surgical peritonitis features ascitic protein >1 g/dL, sugar (glucose) <50 mg/dL, and markedly elevated LDH (LDH ↑↑). (Book p1007)

questions.q: What is the first-line empirical antibiotic regimen recommended for treating spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (SBP), CNNA, and MNNA?
opts: Inj Vancomycin 1 g IV BD plus Metronidazole for 7 days
Inj Cefotaxime 2 g IV TDS for 5 days
Inj Ceftriaxone 1 g IV OD for 14 days
Inj Amoxicillin-clavulanate 1.2 g IV BD for 10 days
questions.exp: The drug and regimen of choice for SBP, CNNA, and MNNA is Inj Cefotaxime 2 g IV TDS for 5 days (printed in text with degraded numeral 'ag IV TDS x 5days'). (Book p1007)

questions.q: A 56-year-old cirrhotic patient recovers successfully from an acute episode of spontaneous bacterial peritonitis. What secondary antibiotic prophylaxis should be instituted upon discharge?
opts: Tab Ciprofloxacin 500 mg BD for 6 months
Tab Rifaximin 550 mg BD lifelong only
Tab Norfloxacin 400 mg OD for life
Tab Norfloxacin 400 mg BD for 7 days
questions.exp: Prophylaxis with Tab Norfloxacin 400 mg OD for life is indicated for: prior SBP, Child-Pugh score ≥9, or ascitic fluid protein <1.5 g/dL in cirrhosis. (Book p1007)

questions.q: In a patient with cirrhosis and ascites presenting with acute upper gastrointestinal (UGI) bleeding, the recommended prophylactic antibiotic regimen to prevent SBP is Tab Norfloxacin ________.
questions.exp: For upper GI bleed in cirrhosis, the specific prophylaxis is Tab Norfloxacin 400 mg BD for 7 days. (Book p1007)

questions.q:
Match each clinical scenario with its recommended Norfloxacin prophylactic regimen:
1. Patient with history of prior SBP
2. Cirrhotic patient with Child's score ≥9 or ascitic protein <1.5 g/dL
3. Cirrhotic patient presenting with acute UGI bleed
opts: 1: 400 mg OD for life; 2: 400 mg OD for life; 3: 400 mg BD for 7 days
1: 400 mg BD for 7 days; 2: 400 mg BD for 7 days; 3: 400 mg OD for life
1: 400 mg OD for life; 2: 400 mg BD for 7 days; 3: 400 mg OD for life
1: 400 mg BD for 14 days; 2: 400 mg OD for life; 3: 400 mg BD for life
questions.exp: Lifelong prophylaxis (Tab Norfloxacin 400 mg OD for life) is indicated for prior SBP, Child's score ≥9, and ascitic fluid protein <1.5 g/dL. Acute UGI bleed warrants short-term prophylaxis: Tab Norfloxacin 400 mg BD for 7 days. (Book p1007)

questions.q: What specific clinical staging and laboratory cutoffs mandate secondary norfloxacin prophylaxis (400 mg OD lifelong) in cirrhotic ascites?
opts: Child's score ≥9 and ascitic fluid protein <1.5 g/dL
Child's score ≥10 and ascitic fluid protein <2.5 g/dL
Child's score ≥7 and ascitic fluid protein <1.0 g/dL
Child's score ≥12 and ascitic fluid protein <0.5 g/dL
questions.exp: Norfloxacin 400 mg OD for life is indicated when the Child-Pugh score is ≥9 or the ascitic fluid protein is <1.5 g/dL in a cirrhotic patient. (Book p1007)

questions.q: What distinguishes diuretic-resistant ascites from diuretic-intractable ascites in patients with chronic liver disease?
opts: Resistant has high SAAG with low protein; intractable has low SAAG with high protein
Resistant fails to respond to full doses; intractable cannot tolerate full doses due to complications
Resistant is caused by portal vein thrombosis; intractable is caused by hepatic vein thrombosis
Resistant responds only to loop diuretics; intractable responds only to aldosterone antagonists
questions.exp: Diuretic-resistant ascites shows no response to full-dose diuretics, whereas diuretic-intractable ascites cannot receive full-dose diuretics due to development of diuretic-induced complications. (Book p1008)

questions.q: Diuretic-resistant ascites is characterized by lack of response to full-dose diuretics, defined in the notes as spironolactone (printed as 40 mg / intended full dose 400 mg) combined with furosemide (Lasix) ________.
questions.exp: In diuretic-resistant ascites, there is no response to full-dose diuretics: spironolactone (printed as 40 mg, full dose 400 mg) plus 160 mg lasix. (Book p1008)

questions.q: Untreated or worsening diuretic-resistant ascites typically progresses directly to which life-threatening complication?
questions.exp: Diuretic resistant ascites is noted as: 'Progresses to HRS'. (Book p1008)

questions.q:
Match each subtype of refractory ascites with its clinical definition and features:
1. Diuretic Resistant Ascites
2. Diuretic Intractable Ascites
opts: 1: Inability to tolerate full doses due to complications like hypo/hyperkalemia or renal failure; 2: Lack of response to full doses (Lasix 160 mg + spironolactone), progresses to HRS
1: Responsive only to salt restriction alone without medications; 2: Complete resolution following a single diagnostic paracentesis
1: Caused by bacterial translocation into the ascitic space; 2: Caused by lymphatic rupture into the peritoneal space
1: Lack of response to full doses (Lasix 160 mg + spironolactone), progresses to HRS; 2: Inability to tolerate full doses due to complications like hypo/hyperkalemia or renal failure
questions.exp: Diuretic resistant ascites is defined by failure to respond to full-dose diuretics and progresses to HRS; diuretic intractable ascites is defined by inability to titrate to full dose due to complications such as electrolyte imbalance (hypo/hyperkalemia) or renal failure. (Book p1008)

questions.q: Diuretic-intractable ascites occurs when full diuretic doses cannot be administered due to medical complications. Which of the following is NOT an example of such a diuretic complication?
questions.exp: Examples given for diuretic-intractable ascites complications are hypokalemia, hyperkalemia, and renal failure. (Book p1008)

questions.q: What definitive interventional radiological procedure is indicated for the management of refractory ascites?
questions.exp: Under refractory ascites, the designated management is TIPSS (Transjugular Intrahepatic Portosystemic Shunt). (Book p1008)

questions.q: In the pathogenesis of hepatorenal syndrome (HRS), what is the initial vascular event that subsequently triggers severe compensatory neurohumoral activation?
questions.exp: Splanchnic vasodilation is the primary event, which stimulates ADH, SNS, and RAAS pathways, resulting in renal vasoconstriction. (Book p1008)

questions.q: In hepatorenal syndrome, splanchnic vasodilation stimulates three primary neurohormonal systems that mediate renal vasoconstriction: ________, ________, and ________.
questions.exp: Splanchnic vasodilation stimulates ADH (antidiuretic hormone), SNS (sympathetic nervous system), and RAAS (renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system). (Book p1008)

questions.q:
Match each hepatorenal syndrome subtype with its progression pathway and clinical outcome:
1. HRS-AKI (Acute Kidney Injury)
2. HRS-NAKI (Non-AKI)
opts: 1: Develops over time in the setting of chronic refractory ascites; 2: Mediated by acute renal vasoconstriction and pre-renal failure, has terrible prognosis with 100% mortality without transplant
1: Resolves spontaneously without medical therapy; 2: Characterized by massive glomerular basement membrane immune deposits
1: Exclusively caused by direct nephrotoxicity of paracetamol; 2: Caused by bacterial invasion of the renal parenchyma
1: Mediated by acute renal vasoconstriction and pre-renal failure, has terrible prognosis with 100% mortality without transplant; 2: Develops over time in the setting of chronic refractory ascites
questions.exp: HRS-AKI arises from severe renal vasoconstriction and pre-renal failure, carrying a terrible prognosis and 100% mortality without liver transplant. HRS-NAKI develops over time in association with refractory ascites. (Book p1008)

questions.q: True or False: In patients who develop HRS-AKI, the prognosis is universally dismal, with 100% mortality expected in the absence of liver transplantation.
opts: False: Fully cured in over 90% of cases by oral loop diuretics alone
False: Fatal only when accompanied by overt hepatic encephalopathy grade 4
True: Terrible prognosis with 100% mortality without liver transplantation
False: Benign self-limiting condition with less than 5% mortality on saline hydration
questions.exp: As emphasized in the text, HRS-AKI has a 'terrible prognosis' and '100% mortality without transplant'. (Book p1008)

questions.q: Hepatorenal syndrome is fundamentally a diagnosis of exclusion established in a patient who must have which foundational underlying clinical triad?
opts: Hepatomegaly, normal portal pressures, and pleural effusion
Acute viral hepatitis, splenomegaly, and macroscopic hematuria
Biliary atresia, normal spleen size, and lower limb edema
questions.exp: HRS is a diagnosis of exclusion in a patient with the triad of Cirrhosis, PHTN, and Ascites. (Book p1008)

questions.q: To confirm hepatorenal syndrome, pre-renal and intra-renal etiologies must be systematically excluded. Which of the following is NOT an intra-renal condition listed in the diagnostic workup?
opts: Structural renal parenchymal abnormalities on USG
Severe hypoalbuminemia (marked reduction in serum albumin)
questions.exp: Marked hypoalbuminemia (↓↓ S. albumin) is classified under pre-renal causes to rule out, along with diuretic excess and UGI bleed. Proteinuria and hematuria are intra-renal markers, and USG rules out structural abnormality. (Book p1008)

questions.q: A 54-year-old man with cirrhosis, ascites, and portal hypertension develops a serum creatinine rise to 2.8 mg/dL. Urinalysis shows no proteinuria or hematuria, renal ultrasonography shows normal kidney morphology, there is no history of shock or nephrotoxic drug ingestion, and diuretic withdrawal with volume expansion does not reverse the renal dysfunction. This confirms:
opts: Primary bilateral polycystic kidney disease complicated by infected renal cysts
Hepatorenal syndrome diagnosed after ruling out pre-renal, intra-renal, and structural etiologies
Acute post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis with persistent nephrotic proteinuria
Contrast-induced acute tubular necrosis responding rapidly to furosemide diuresis
questions.exp: HRS is a diagnosis of exclusion in a patient with cirrhosis, PHTN, and ascites after ruling out pre-renal failure (diuretic excess, UGI bleed, hypoalbuminemia), intra-renal disease (proteinuria, hematuria), structural abnormalities on USG, shock, and nephrotoxic drugs (diuretics, NSAIDs). (Book p1008)

questions.q:
Match the diagnostic exclusion category with the specific factors that must be ruled out when evaluating for HRS:
1. Pre-renal etiologies
2. Intra-renal etiologies
3. Nephrotoxic exposures
opts: 1: Structural abnormalities on USG; 2: NSAIDs; 3: Marked hypoalbuminemia and hematuria
1: Diuretics and NSAIDs; 2: Diuretic excess; 3: Proteinuria and hematuria
1: Diuretic excess, marked hypoalbuminemia, and UGI bleed; 2: Proteinuria and hematuria; 3: Diuretics and NSAIDs
1: Proteinuria and hematuria; 2: Diuretic excess and UGI bleed; 3: Hypoalbuminemia and shock
questions.exp: Pre-renal factors to rule out are diuretic excess, severe hypoalbuminemia (↓↓ S. albumin), and UGI bleed; intra-renal factors are proteinuria and hematuria; nephrotoxic drugs include diuretics and NSAIDs. (Book p1008)

questions.q: What is the definitive and curative management for hepatorenal syndrome (HRS)?
questions.exp: Liver transplantation is the definitive management for hepatorenal syndrome. (Book p1009)

questions.q: What is the recommended dosing and titration schedule for intravenous terlipressin used to reverse splanchnic vasodilation prior to liver transplantation in HRS?
opts: 0.5 mg IV continuous infusion doubling every 24 hours (max 6 mg/day)
4 mg IV every 8 hours with rapid taper after 48 hours (max 16 mg/day)
1 mg IV every 4–6 hours, titrating up to 2 mg IV every 4–6 hours (max 12 mg/day)
2 mg IV stat followed by 1 mg IV every 12 hours (maximum 4 mg/day)
questions.exp: Terlipressin is administered as 1 mg IV every 4-6 hours, titrated up to 2 mg IV every 4-6 hours, with a maximum dose of 12 mg/day. (Book p1009)

questions.q: Which medical regimens are used to counter splanchnic vasodilation and serve as a pharmacological bridge to liver transplantation in HRS?
opts: Dopamine infusion, oral furosemide, and intravenous loop diuretics
Nitroprusside, oral hydralazine, and intravenous labetalol
Terlipressin, subcutaneous Octreotide plus oral Midodrine, or Norepinephrine
questions.exp: Medical therapy to prevent splanchnic vasodilation until transplant includes: Terlipressin, subcutaneous Octreotide + oral Midodrine (oral alpha agonist), or Norepinephrine. (Book p1009)

questions.q: In the medical management of hepatorenal syndrome, midodrine is administered as an ________ and functions pharmacologically as an ________.
questions.exp: Midodrine is an oral alpha-agonist (oral α agonist) used in combination with subcutaneous octreotide. (Book p1009)

questions.q: A 49-year-old patient with decompensated cirrhosis and type 1 hepatorenal syndrome (HRS-AKI) is listed for urgent orthotopic liver transplantation. While awaiting donor organ availability, what medical regimen should be instituted immediately to reverse splanchnic vasodilation?
opts: Aggressive volume resuscitation with 5% dextrose and forced furosemide diuresis
Empirical high-dose oral spironolactone 400 mg daily with potassium chloride
Bilateral renal denervation via catheter-based radiofrequency ablation
Terlipressin 1 mg IV Q4-6H titrated up to 2 mg Q4-6H (or octreotide plus midodrine)
questions.exp: Medical management to counter splanchnic vasodilation until liver transplant includes terlipressin (1 mg IV Q4-6h up to 2 mg Q4-6h, max 12 mg/d), octreotide plus midodrine, or norepinephrine. (Book p1009)

questions.q:
Match each pharmacological agent used in hepatorenal syndrome with its specific administration detail:
1. Terlipressin
2. Midodrine
3. Octreotide
opts: 1: 1 mg IV Q4-6h titrating to 2 mg IV Q4-6h (max 12 mg/d); 2: Oral alpha agonist; 3: Subcutaneous (S/C) administration
1: Subcutaneous administration; 2: 1 mg IV Q4-6h (max 12 mg/d); 3: Oral alpha agonist
1: Oral alpha agonist; 2: Subcutaneous administration; 3: 1 mg IV Q4-6h titrating to 2 mg
1: 1 mg IV Q4-6h; 2: Subcutaneous administration; 3: Oral alpha agonist
questions.exp: Terlipressin is given IV 1 mg Q4-6h up to 2 mg Q4-6h (max 12 mg/d); midodrine is an oral alpha agonist; octreotide is given subcutaneously (S/C) in combination with midodrine. (Book p1009)

questions.q: In hepatopulmonary syndrome (HPS), chronic liver disease leads to excessive pulmonary production of which potent gaseous vasodilator?
questions.exp: Chronic liver disease stimulates excess nitric oxide (NO) production, resulting in intrapulmonary capillary dilatation. (Book p1009)

questions.q: In hepatopulmonary syndrome, what is the extent of intrapulmonary capillary dilatation compared to normal pulmonary capillary diameter?
questions.exp: Pulmonary capillary diameter expands dramatically from normal 8-15 µm up to 50-500 µm in HPS. (Book p1009)

questions.q: The marked intrapulmonary capillary dilatation in HPS leads to decreased oxygenation and arteriovenous shunts, causing hypoxia/hypoxemia via ________.
questions.exp: The combination of decreased oxygenation and AV shunts causes hypoxia/hypoxemia through ventilation-perfusion (V/Q) mismatch. (Book p1009)

questions.q: Platypnea is defined as dyspnea provoked by standing upright. What are the two physiological factors identified in the text that produce platypnea in HPS?
opts: Pulmonary capillary constriction and diaphragm descent
Increased AV shunt activation and diaphragm moving up
Decreased bronchial caliber and left ventricular failure
Carotid sinus denervation and alveolar collapse
questions.exp: Platypnea is dyspnea on standing due to: (1) ↑ AV shunt activation and (2) diaphragm moves up. (Book p1009)

questions.q: Orthodeoxia is a hallmark clinical sign of hepatopulmonary syndrome defined by which specific arterial oxygen saturation change on standing?
questions.exp: Orthodeoxia is explicitly defined as a drop of SpO2 > 3% on standing. (Book p1009)

questions.q: What is the investigation of choice (IOC) to demonstrate intrapulmonary vascular dilatations in hepatopulmonary syndrome?
opts: Invasive right heart catheterization with pulmonary angiography
questions.exp: The investigation of choice (IOC) for HPS is Bubble Echocardiography / Contrast Transthoracic Echocardiography. (Book p1009)

questions.q: What is the definitive curative treatment for hepatopulmonary syndrome (HPS)?
questions.exp: The definitive treatment for HPS is liver transplantation. (Book p1009)

questions.q: A 50-year-old woman with cirrhosis complains of progressive shortness of breath when sitting up, improving when lying flat. Pulse oximetry reveals SpO2 of 96% supine, dropping to 91% on standing. Bubble echocardiography is positive for intrapulmonary shunting. What is the diagnosis and definitive management?
opts: Large hepatic hydrothorax; Tube thoracostomy and chemical pleurodesis
Portopulmonary hypertension; Sildenafil and bosentan therapy
Hepatorenal syndrome type 1; Terlipressin and albumin infusion
questions.exp: The triad of chronic liver disease, platypnea-orthodeoxia (drop in SpO2 > 3% on standing), and positive bubble echocardiography confirms hepatopulmonary syndrome (HPS), for which the definitive treatment is liver transplantation. (Book p1009)

units.title: Pathophysiology & Ascitic Fluid Characterization

units.title: Clinical Examination, Paracentesis & Medical Grading
units.guide: Apply anatomical landmarks for paracentesis, fluid detection thresholds, and graded step-up therapy from salt restriction to diuretics.

units.guide: Identify diagnostic cutoffs for SBP and distinguish CNNA and MNNA variants based on neutrophil counts and microbiology.

units.title: Management, Surgical Peritonitis & SBP Prophylaxis
units.guide: Differentiate surgical peritonitis from SBP, apply empirical cefotaxime regimens, and determine indications for norfloxacin prophylaxis.

units.title: Refractory Ascites: Subtypes & Procedural Interventions
units.guide: Distinguish diuretic-resistant from diuretic-intractable ascites and identify indications for TIPSS.

units.title: Hepatorenal Syndrome: Pathophysiology, Diagnosis & Management
units.guide: Follow the vasoconstrictive progression from splanchnic dilation to renal failure, apply diagnostic exclusion criteria, and institute terlipressin bridge therapy.

units.title: Hepatopulmonary Syndrome: Pulmonary Vascular Complications
units.guide: Recognize nitric oxide-driven intrapulmonary capillary dilatation, platypnea-orthodeoxia, bubble echocardiography findings, and definitive liver transplantation.
